o1.biggest_strength: The numbers are worked step by step and all check out. It also builds in a 50/50 portal test and a 10% holdout, and it admits that fit-finder users chose the quiz themselves by closing only half the 19-point gap.
o1.biggest_mistake: It gives single-point estimates (tickets halved, 35% swap share) instead of an honest range. It has no short day-3 'still on track' nudge and no fit guidance for first-time bra buyers after delivery, only a generic 'swap my size' email.
o1.what_would_make_it_a_10: Show low and high ranges, add a day-3 status message, and put real how-to-check-your-fit guidance in the post-delivery bra email.

o2.biggest_strength: It opens with the cost of the problem (£139,800 in returns, £31,360 in tickets) and gives low-to-high ranges for every lever. It also covers every message the owner hoped for, including a day-3 update and a bra-specific fit-check email after delivery.
o2.biggest_mistake: The swap-first headline of 'up to £183,800 in sales kept' is a loose upper bound. The portal pre-selects swap for size reasons, which edges toward a nudge, and it has no explicit portal A/B test.
o2.what_would_make_it_a_10: Add a controlled test of the new portal against the old one, and use a firmer, more cautious figure for sales kept.

reason: Both plans have correct maths and good copy. Number 2 has honest ranges, the day-3 nudge, more useful fit guidance in the post-delivery bra email, and a clear 8-week order of work, so it fits what I asked for slightly better.
